prompt: Order the six phases of incident response this course follows.
What changed with NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3, published in April 2025?

choices.text: It added a seventh phase, threat hunting
choices.why: Hunting is not a phase in either model.

choices.text: It replaced incident response with SOAR
choices.why: Automation is not the subject of the change.

choices.text: It made the four phases of Revision 2 mandatory for every federal contractor in the United States
choices.why: It superseded Revision 2 and dropped the cycle as its organising idea.

choices.text: It maps response onto the CSF 2.0 functions instead of a four-phase cycle
choices.why: Right. Preparation becomes governance and protection that run all the time.

prompt: Why does containment often start before identification is finished?

choices.text: NIST forbids it
choices.why: Neither model forbids overlap.

choices.text: A P1 cannot wait
choices.why: Right. Phases overlap in practice.

choices.text: Identification is optional
choices.why: It continues; it is not skipped.

choices.text: The plan requires containment within ten minutes of any alert, whatever its priority
choices.why: No such rule exists in the lesson's plan.

prompt: At two in the morning, the analyst on call sees data leaving the file server. The plan says nothing about who may isolate it. What happens, according to the lesson?

choices.text: The SIEM isolates it automatically
choices.why: Nothing in the course gives the SIEM that power.

choices.text: They wait for a director and lose hours, or act without authority and take the blame
choices.why: Right. That is why authority is delegated in advance.

choices.text: They follow the NIST default, which allows isolation
choices.why: There is no such default.

choices.text: Nothing, because isolation is never needed at night
choices.why: The transfer was at 02:41.

prompt: Why should an incident response plan be short?

choices.text: Short plans need no review, so they save time for the team in quiet periods
choices.why: Every plan is reviewed yearly and after incidents.

choices.text: Auditors penalise long documents
choices.why: The reason is use, not audit.

choices.text: It is read mid-incident
choices.why: Right. A long plan is an unread plan.

choices.text: So that it fits in the SIEM
choices.why: The SIEM does not hold the plan.

prompt: Match each part of the plan to the question it settles.

pairs.right: how do they talk if email is not trusted?
who outside helps, and who must be told?
where do the hashed logs go?

prompt: Which role do small teams skip most often, according to the lesson, and what is lost?

choices.text: IT operations; nothing is ever changed
choices.why: Not the lesson's point.

choices.text: The executive sponsor; nobody pays for the tools
choices.why: The lesson names the scribe and the lead/typist split.

choices.text: Legal; the plan becomes illegal
choices.why: A plan does not become illegal for lack of a lawyer in the room.

choices.text: The scribe; the response cannot be reconstructed or defended later
choices.why: Right. The decision log feeds lesson 20's report.

prompt: Why is bruno not on the response team for this incident?

choices.text: He is in finance
choices.why: His department is not the reason.

choices.text: He is a witness and possibly a victim, not an investigator of his own case
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: He is suspected of a crime and has been dismissed by the company
choices.why: Nothing says so; he may be the victim.

choices.text: He does not know Linux
choices.why: Skill is not the reason.

prompt: Why does the lesson separate the incident lead from the person typing commands?

choices.text: Nobody types and watches at once
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Typing is a junior's job and leading is for directors, as in any hierarchy
choices.why: It is about attention, not rank.

choices.text: Leads are not allowed to have shell access
choices.why: Access is not the issue.

choices.text: The law requires two people
choices.why: No law in the lesson.

prompt: Match each document to its kind.

pairs.left: how to image a disk with dd
how to disable an account in the directory

prompt: The playbook says to confirm with the account's owner by a channel other than that account. Why?

choices.text: Email is too slow for an incident of priority one
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: The owner is not allowed to read email during an incident
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: Whoever controls the account would answer instead
choices.why: Right. A phone call or a face-to-face question.

choices.text: To keep the SIEM quiet
choices.why: The SIEM is not the concern.

prompt: A runbook for isolating a server was written two years ago and never run. What is the likeliest outcome when it is first used during an incident?

choices.text: The SIEM refuses to let anybody run it
choices.why: The SIEM does not run runbooks.

choices.text: Legal has to approve it first
choices.why: Not what the lesson warns about.

choices.text: A step fails because something it names has changed
choices.why: Right. Test runbooks when written, and again when systems change.

choices.text: It works, since runbooks do not age
choices.why: Interfaces, names and tools change underneath them.

prompt: Why does the jump bag hold the plan and the contacts on paper or offline?

choices.text: Paper cannot be lost
choices.why: It can; it just does not depend on the network.

choices.text: Paper is easier to search than a shared drive, especially for a plan with many pages
choices.why: Searchability is not the reason.

choices.text: Auditors require paper
choices.why: Not the reason given.

choices.text: The systems holding them are what an incident hits
choices.why: Right.

prompt: What problem do break-glass accounts prevent during containment?

choices.text: The SIEM filling its disk
choices.why: Unrelated.

choices.text: The intruder finding the plan on the company's shared drive and reading the response
choices.why: That is what out-of-band communication addresses.

choices.text: Admins locked out
choices.why: Right. A classic self-inflicted outage.

choices.text: Evidence being changed
choices.why: That is the write blocker's job.

prompt: What is the output of a tabletop exercise?

choices.text: A list of gaps with owners and dates
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Changes made on the live systems
choices.why: Nothing is touched in a tabletop.

choices.text: A signed approval of the plan
choices.why: It finds gaps rather than approving.

choices.text: A score for each participant, so the company knows who responded best and can promote them
choices.why: It tests the plan, not the people.

prompt: Every answer in a tabletop was in the plan and nobody hesitated. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: A good one is mildly uncomfortable.

choices.text: The scenario was written too easily
choices.why: Right. It should probe the gaps.

choices.text: The plan should be shortened
choices.why: Its length is not what the exercise measured.

choices.text: Tabletops are no longer needed and the next one can be cancelled
choices.why: Run at least yearly.

choices.text: The company is fully prepared
choices.why: One easy exercise does not prove that.
